content.title: Artemis II's landing may be the most dangerous part of the mission | Former astronaut raises concerns as NASA assures safety
content.text: The heat shield is critical to protect the crew when they reenter the atmosphere on Friday, and it was heavily damaged during the previous Artemis mission. CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — An astronaut is sounding the alarm ahead of the Artemis II mission's reentry on Friday, claiming NASA's failure to fix a critical issue is putting the crew's safety in jeopardy. Astronaut Charles Camarda, who was formerly the senior adviser for innovation at Johnson Space Center, made the claims after poring over documents related to the Artemis program. Camarda was previously in charge of evaluating problems and guiding safety protocols for NASA programs. Camarda claims the Artemis II crew's safety is at risk because a mechanical failure that took place on the uncrewed 2022 Artemis I mission hadn't properly been fixed. When the Artemis I reentered the atmosphere after its mission around the moon, it returned with a seriously damaged heat shield. The NASA analysis of the Artemis I heat shield's failure alleged that gases generated inside the heat shield's outer material, during a new re-entry technique, weren't able to vent properly, leading to pressure building up, cracking occurring, and charred material breaking off in several locations. NASA's solution to the problem was to modify the spacecraft's trajectory upon reentry, without replacing or changing the heat shield's materials. But Camarda claims the tools NASA used to analyze the problem are "woefully inadequate" to understand the problem and even compared them to the tools that were to blame for the Challenger disaster and the loss of the Columbia space shuttle. Camarda said the true cause of Artemis I's heat shield damage was due to an inherent structural failure, rather than the new entry technique causing gases to build up. He also claimed NASA never revealed the modified trajectory to the public. Camarda said that various failures in NASA's management of the program, including dysfunctional organizational behaviors and poor engineering training, exacerbated the problems. "We are trying to prevent the loss of the Artemis II crew," Camarda said. "History does not repeat because engineers forget equations. It repeats because organizations forget how to listen to them." Other NASA representatives have echoed the agency's explanation of the problem. Former NASA Associate Administrator James Free, who retired from the agency in 2025, said the agency took time to understand what the root cause of the heat shield's failure was, and engineers determined that they could launch the Artemis II mission without changing out the heat shield, saying the crew was "well within" safety parameters. "It's all how you enter the atmosphere," Free said during a recent interview. "If you limit the angle at which [Artemis] comes in, that limits how far down range you can go, which limits your landing attempts, but you still stay within the temperature limits that you need to for Artemis II, and that's what they have planned." NASA also said the temperature data from inside Artemis I held steady in the mid-70s during the heat shield's issues, saying it "exceeded expectations." The Artemis II mission is scheduled to splash down off San Diego's coast just after 5 p.m. PT on Friday.
